transcript.content: Hello, I’m Dr. __. What brings you in today?

Hi, Dr. __. Yeah, um, well, I’m here because... for almost two years now, I’ve just been unable to shake this absolute certainty about my ensemble. It all started right after this big commission we did. 

Which, honestly, was a whole ordeal on its own because the venue they booked us in had this awful acoustic dead zone near the back wall. I actually had to completely re-voice the brass section just so the French horns wouldn't get swallowed up by the heavy velvet curtains they refused to take down. It took me weeks of late nights just to fix the acoustics on paper. I practically lived on this terrible burnt diner coffee from down the street—you know the kind that tastes like pennies? 

But anyway, sorry... the point is, ever since that commission, a few people in the ensemble started quietly trying to undermine my work. It's always these subtle things, you know? Sudden schedule changes, weird seating choices, or just these little, pointed comments during rehearsals. And they always have a perfectly constructed excuse. They’ll pull out their phones and show me emails or administrative notes that supposedly explain it all away, like, "Oh, the hall was double-booked" or "the union required a break." But I know what they're actually doing. It reminds me of when I was in grad school and my roommate kept moving my manuscript paper just an inch to the left every single day. You just know when people are deliberately messing with your head.
Do you think there is any real possibility that your ensemble members are not trying to undermine you?

I mean... I try to be objective about it. I really do. But for almost two years now, ever since that big commission, I’ve just been completely unable to shake the certainty that it's intentional. A few people in the ensemble are definitely using those schedule changes, the weird seating choices, and those little comments during rehearsals to quietly undermine my work. I know they show me emails or administrative notes that supposedly explain it all away, but... it's just too consistent, you know? 

It’s exactly like when you’re tuning a cello and the peg keeps slipping just a fraction of a millimeter. Did I tell you about my old principal cellist, Marcus? He had this gorgeous 19th-century instrument—French, I think—but the pegs were an absolute nightmare. We were playing this outdoor festival in July, which, by the way, is the worst possible idea for string instruments. The humidity just completely destroys the intonation. We had to keep stopping every eight bars just to re-tune. I actually told the festival organizers months in advance that we needed a climate-controlled tent, but they completely ignored me because of the budget. They always blame the budget, don't they? It's like pulling teeth trying to get decent arts funding in this city. I spent three hours on the phone with the city council once just trying to get a permit for a generator... 

But anyway, wait, what was I... what did you ask me? Oh, right, about them not trying to undermine me. Yeah, no, even with their supposed proof and the emails they show me, I just know what they're actually doing.
Have you ever changed your mind about this belief after someone showed you clear evidence that it might not be true?

Change my mind? No. Like I was just saying, even when they shove those emails or administrative notes right in my face to supposedly explain it all away, it doesn't change anything. I just can't shake the certainty. It’s been almost two years since that commission, and I know they are using those schedule shifts, the seating choices, the little comments to quietly undermine my work. 

The emails don't prove anything. Actually, speaking of emails, you wouldn't believe the server issues we had at the conservatory right around that time. The IT department decided to migrate the entire faculty to a new cloud system right in the middle of jury week. Jury week! I had seventy-five undergraduate composition portfolios to review, and the whole system just completely locked me out. I spent four hours sitting in the basement IT office with this guy... Todd, I think? He had this massive collection of vintage synthesizers on his desk, which was actually pretty incredible. We started talking about the Moog Sub 37 and how that raw analog warmth just cannot be replicated by digital plugins, no matter what the software developers claim. I actually wrote a piece for a Moog and string quartet once, but the cellist refused to play with a click track, so the tempo sync was just a complete disaster live... 

Wait, did I already say that? What were we talking about? Oh, right, the proof. Yeah, no, their supposed evidence doesn't change my mind at all.
Have you ever heard voices or seen things that other people could not?

Voices? Or seeing things? No, definitely not. I mean, I hear music in my head pretty much constantly, but that's just normal composer stuff, you know? Not like actual voices or anything. 

Although, speaking of hearing things, we had this one tenor in the chorale last spring who swore he heard a metronome clicking during our performance of the Mozart Requiem. It was driving him absolutely crazy. But it turned out it was just the HVAC system in this old cathedral we were performing in. That church was visually stunning, stained glass everywhere, but the heating system was practically prehistoric. It would kick on with this heavy, rhythmic clunk-hiss, clunk-hiss sound. I actually ended up recording it on my phone because the rhythm fell into this perfect 5/8 time signature. 

I really wanted to sample it for an electronic percussion piece I was working on, but getting clean audio in that space was totally impossible because of the reverb. The acoustic decay in there was like four seconds long. You absolutely cannot write fast counterpoint for a room like that, it just turns into acoustic mud. Bach really knew what he was doing writing for those big stone spaces, you have to completely stretch out the harmonic rhythm or else the frequencies just crash into each other and... um. 

Wait. Sorry, what was I just saying? Did you ask about the cathedral? Oh, right, voices. Yeah, no, I don't hear or see anything that isn't actually there. Just the usual ensemble drama.
Have you noticed any other unusual beliefs that other people would think are strange or impossible?

Other unusual beliefs? No, I don't think so. I mean, people might think it's strange that I know they're undermining me, but it's not impossible, it's just what's happening. I don't have any, like, bizarre conspiracy theories or anything like that. 

Although, speaking of strange beliefs, my old composition professor had this absolute obsession with the golden ratio. Like, it went way beyond just analyzing Bartók. He would literally measure the margins of our manuscript paper with a ruler to make sure they fit the Fibonacci sequence. If they didn't, he wouldn't even look at the piece. He claimed it affected the visual resonance of the score, which, honestly, is just ridiculous. I mean, sure, the golden ratio is a fascinating structural tool—I actually used it to dictate the entry points of the fugue subject in my master's thesis—but to apply it to the physical paper? 

My thesis defense, actually, was a whole other ordeal. One of the panelists got stuck in an elevator in the music building for two hours. The fire department had to come pry the doors open. It was the same elevator that always gets stuck between the third and fourth floors, right by the percussion studios. You'd think with the tuition they charge, they could fix an elevator, but no, all the money goes to the football team. It's a complete joke. The athletic director makes like five times what the dean of the music school makes...

Wait, sorry, I lost my train of thought again. What were we talking about? Oh, right, other strange beliefs. No, just the thing with the ensemble. Everything else is totally normal.
Have you been having trouble keeping your thoughts organized or speaking in a way that others can follow?

Trouble keeping my thoughts organized? Or speaking so people can follow? No, I don't think so. I mean, my thoughts are perfectly clear to me. I communicate just fine, especially when I'm working with the ensemble. You have to be incredibly precise when you're directing, you know? 

Like, just last week, I was trying to explain this very specific articulation I wanted from the brass section in this contemporary piece we're doing. It’s this really jagged, asymmetrical meter, and they were just playing it way too legato. I had to stop them like four times. The trumpet player—he's this guy who always wears these incredibly loud, vintage Hawaiian shirts to rehearsal, which is honestly so distracting. I don't know where he even finds them. He told me once he gets them from this thrift store three towns over that specializes in mid-century resort wear. Which is a weirdly specific business model, if you think about it. Who is buying enough vintage resort wear in the Midwest to keep a store like that open? 

Anyway, I went to a thrift store once looking for a specific kind of vintage lamp for my studio, because the overhead fluorescents give me a terrible headache. I ended up finding this amazing old rotary phone instead. It doesn't work, obviously, but the aesthetic is just fantastic. I put it right next to my MIDI controller. It’s a funny contrast, you know? The analog past right next to the digital future...

Wait, sorry. Did I drift off again? What was the question? Oh, right, keeping my thoughts organized. Yeah, no, I don't have any trouble with that. People follow me just fine.
In the past two years, have you ever felt unusually suspicious or fearful in other areas of your life, outside of the ensemble?

Suspicious outside the ensemble? No, not at all. Outside of this whole issue with them, my life is completely normal. I'm still hitting all my deadlines, keeping up with my composing, and I run most mornings. 

Actually, my morning run is where I get some of my best ideas. I take this route down by the river, past this old industrial bakery. The smell of the yeast fermenting in the early morning is incredible—it's this deep, sour, earthy scent. It always makes me think about the fermentation process, you know, how it's basically just controlled decay. Which is a really fascinating concept to apply to musical form. I've been trying to write a string quartet based on that idea, where the primary motif slowly breaks down over the course of twenty minutes. It's tricky, though, because if you decay the motif too quickly, the audience loses the thread, and if you do it too slowly, it's just boring. 

I was explaining this to my wife over breakfast—things at home with her are basically steady, by the way, she's been great. She actually bought me these new running shoes for my birthday because my old ones were completely worn through on the left heel. It's weird how I overpronate on just one side. The guy at the shoe store said it's probably because of how I shift my weight when I stand on the podium to conduct. He used to be a physical therapist before he opened the running shop, which seems like a pretty drastic career change, but I guess if you love shoes... 

Wait, sorry. Did I get off track again? What were you asking about? Oh, being fearful. No, no. Like I said, everything outside the ensemble is totally fine.
Have you ever had any periods of feeling unusually high, energized, or irritable around the same time as this belief?

Unusually high or energized? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I have normal energy levels. Sometimes I get a little irritable, sure, but that's just because they're actively trying to ruin my career, which would make anyone irritable. But not like, unusually high energy or anything. 

I do drink a lot of coffee, though. Probably too much. There's this little cafe near the conservatory that pulls the most incredible espresso. The barista there, she's actually a percussion major, she told me they source their beans from this tiny cooperative in Guatemala. They roast them locally, like, right in the back of the shop. You can actually hear the roaster going if you sit near the bathroom. It sounds a lot like a snare drum roll, actually, just this low, continuous rumble. I tried recording it once on my phone to use as a sample in an electronic piece, but the audio quality was terrible. Phone microphones just can't capture those low frequencies properly. You really need a good condenser mic for that kind of field recording. 

My friend David—he does sound design for video games—he has this whole setup he carries around in a specialized backpack. He was telling me about this game he worked on where they needed the sound of a dragon breathing fire, and he ended up recording a blowtorch inside a metal trash can. Isn't that wild? The things people come up with. He makes a really good living doing it, too. Sometimes I wonder if I should have gone into commercial music instead of contemporary classical. There's definitely more money in dragons than in string quartets...

Wait, sorry. I'm doing it again, aren't I? Getting off track. What was the question? Oh, right, feeling high or energized. No, no, my energy is totally normal. Just the usual amount of stress from, you know, the situation with the ensemble.
Have you had any other fixed beliefs that people around you say are not true?

Other fixed beliefs? Like, things people say aren't true? No, it's just this one thing with the ensemble. Everyone agrees about everything else. I mean, my wife and I might disagree on small things, like what color to paint the living room, but that's normal. 

Actually, speaking of paint, we were at the hardware store this weekend looking at swatches, and the sheer number of whites they have is staggering. There’s "Navajo White," "Eggshell," "Alabaster"... I was looking at one called "Cloud Nine," and it just looked slightly yellow to me. The guy working in the paint department—he had this really intense, bushy mustache, like Tom Selleck in the 80s—he was explaining how the base tint affects the way the light reflects off it. He said something about the undertones, how a blue undertone makes it look cooler, but a red undertone warms it up. 

It made me think about orchestration, actually. How if you double a melody in the flutes, it gives it this cool, bright edge, but if you double it in the horns, it suddenly has this warm, resonant depth. It's all about the undertones, right? The overtones, technically, in music. I had this acoustics professor in undergrad who was obsessed with the overtone series. He built this giant, custom monochord in his garage just to demonstrate how the string divides into nodes. He brought it into class one day, and it took up half the room. It sounded terrible, just this dull thud when he plucked it, but the physics of it were fascinating...

Wait, sorry. I drifted off again. What were we talking about? Oh, right, other beliefs people say aren't true. No, no, nothing else. Just the situation with the ensemble.
Have you ever experienced any strange sensations, like hearing your name when no one is there, or feeling like something is touching or moving around you when it isn’t?

Strange sensations? Hearing my name? No, I haven't had anything like that. No voices, no feeling like I'm being touched. My hearing is actually very acute, which is both a blessing and a curse in my line of work. 

I was actually just getting my hearing checked last month, just a routine audiogram. You have to protect your ears when you're around brass instruments all day. The audiologist had this incredibly quiet booth. I mean, the sound isolation was phenomenal. You sit in there, and the silence is almost deafening, if that makes sense. It reminded me of this piece by John Cage, 4'33", where the performer just sits at the piano and doesn't play a single note for four minutes and thirty-three seconds. The idea is that the ambient noise in the concert hall—the coughing, the shifting in seats, the HVAC system—becomes the music. 

I tried programming it once for a student recital, but the administration threw a fit. They said parents wouldn't understand why they paid tuition for their kids to sit in silence. Which totally misses the point of the piece, but you know how administrators are. They only care about the bottom line. The dean of the music school, he used to be an accountant before he went into higher ed administration. He always wears these really loud, mismatched ties. Like, a polka dot tie with a striped shirt. It's visually jarring. I don't know how his wife lets him leave the house like that...

Oh, I'm sorry. I'm rambling again, aren't I? You asked about hearing voices or feeling things. No, nothing like that at all. Just my normal, very sensitive hearing.
Outside of the ensemble, have you ever had any other beliefs that other people would consider clearly false or impossible?

Other beliefs? Like, impossible things? No, definitely not. I mean, I'm a very rational person. Everything else in my life is completely grounded in reality. It's really just this one specific issue with the ensemble trying to force me out. 

Although, speaking of impossible things, I was reading this article the other day about quantum entanglement. Have you heard of it? It's this phenomenon where two particles become linked, and whatever happens to one instantly affects the other, even if they're light-years apart. Einstein called it "spooky action at a distance." It's completely counterintuitive, right? It violates everything we understand about classical physics and the speed of light. 

I was trying to explain it to my cellist—well, the one who isn't actively conspiring against me—and she just looked at me like I was speaking Greek. She's incredibly talented, absolute perfect pitch, but her interests are very... narrow. She only reads biographies of 19th-century Russian composers. Which is fine, I guess, but there's a whole universe out there. She actually has this antique cello, made in Cremona in the 1700s. The varnish on it is this deep, rich amber color. She refuses to check it when she flies, she actually buys a separate seat for it. I saw her arguing with a flight attendant once because they wanted her to put it in the overhead bin. Can you imagine? Shoving a three-hundred-year-old instrument into an overhead bin next to someone's smelly gym bag...

Wait, sorry. I'm doing it again. Tangents. You asked about other false beliefs. No, absolutely not. Just the very real situation with the ensemble. Everything else is completely normal.
Have you been feeling depressed or down most of the time during the same period that you’ve had this belief?

Depressed? Down? No, not really. I mean, the situation with the ensemble is incredibly frustrating, obviously, but it hasn't made me depressed. 

Actually, speaking of being down, we were just debating whether to program Mahler's *Kindertotenlieder* for the winter vocal series. It translates to "Songs on the Death of Children," which is... well, you can't really get more depressing than that, can you? It's a gorgeous cycle, musically speaking, but it's incredibly heavy for an audience. The mezzo-soprano we usually hire for these things, Sarah, she has this incredibly dark, velvety lower register that would be perfect for it. But she just got a rescue dog, this little terrier mix, and she insists on bringing it to every rehearsal. She puts it in this little canvas tote bag. It's actually very well-behaved, it mostly just sleeps under her chair, but our principal oboist is terribly allergic to dogs. He started sneezing in the middle of a very delicate solo last week. It completely ruined the phrasing. 

He's so particular, too. He uses these custom-made reeds that he shaves down himself with this tiny, terrifyingly sharp knife. I watched him do it once in the green room, and the precision required is just astounding. One wrong scrape and the whole piece of cane is ruined. He buys the cane straight from this specific farm in the south of France, and he was telling me how the soil composition there affects the density of the wood. Apparently, if there's too much rain in the spring, the cane gets too porous and it completely changes the vibrato... 

Anyway, sorry, I'm drifting again. You were asking about my mood? No, I'm not depressed. Just... focused on my work, and trying to manage the people who are actively trying to undermine it.
Has anything happened that seems clearly impossible or bizarre to you, not just suspicious or hurtful?

Impossible or bizarre? No, no, nothing like that. Like I said, I'm a very rational person. The things happening with the ensemble are very real, very grounded in reality. There's no magic or aliens or anything bizarre going on. 

Although, you know what is bizarre? The way the acoustics work in the new performance hall downtown. Have you been there yet? The architecture is stunning, all this curved glass and blonde wood, but the acoustic design is just completely baffling. There's this one dead spot right in the middle of the second tier where if you're sitting there, the brass section sounds like they're playing underwater. I was talking to the acoustic engineer they hired—he's this Swedish guy who wears these tiny, perfectly round glasses—and he was trying to explain how the sound waves are reflecting off the glass panels at the wrong angle. 

He was using all these complex mathematical models on his tablet, showing me the sound decay rates. It's fascinating how much math goes into designing a room just so people can hear a violin properly. He actually designed this incredible hall in Tokyo a few years ago where the seats are arranged in a vineyard style, so the audience surrounds the stage. I've always wanted to conduct in a space like that. It completely changes the dynamic between the musicians and the audience when they're sitting behind you, watching your face instead of your back. I have this one baton, it's carbon fiber with a cork handle, perfectly balanced, and I always wonder if the audience behind me would be able to see the tiny, micro-movements I make with it...

But, uh, anyway. Bizarre things. No. Just the very real, very concrete conspiracy to push me out of my job. Nothing impossible about that, unfortunately.
Have you ever believed that someone was controlling your thoughts or actions?

Controlling my thoughts? Or actions? No. No, that's... no, I'm the one in control of my own mind. I'm a conductor, my entire profession is about controlling my own actions to guide others. 

Speaking of conducting, I actually had to change my rehearsal technique recently because of a shoulder issue. I was reading this fascinating study on the biomechanics of conducting—did you know that the repetitive stress injuries conductors get are actually very similar to what baseball pitchers experience? It's all in the rotator cuff. I had to start doing these highly specific physical therapy exercises with resistance bands. My physical therapist, David, he's this former college swimmer, incredibly intense guy. He has this massive chart of the human muscular system on his wall, and he was pointing out exactly which tiny stabilizing muscles I was neglecting. 

He actually recommended I try swimming to build up the supporting musculature. I haven't been swimming since I was a kid. My parents used to take me to this public pool in the summer, and the smell of the chlorine was just overwhelming. They had this diving board that was slightly loose, so it made this distinct rattling sound every time someone jumped off it. I can still hear the exact pitch of it, actually, it was a slightly flat F sharp...

Oh, sorry. Tangents again. But no, to answer your question, nobody is controlling my thoughts or actions. My mind is my own. It's just the ensemble situation that's the problem.
What, exactly, do you believe your ensemble is doing to undermine you?

Well, it's been going on for almost two years now, ever since that big commission we did. I'm absolutely certain that a few specific people in the ensemble are quietly trying to push me out. They do it through these little, calculated moves—sudden schedule changes that I'm barely looped in on, very deliberate seating choices during rehearsals, and these subtle, undermining comments when we're working on a piece. And I know what you're going to say, they show me emails or rehearsal notes that supposedly explain it all away as logistical issues, but I know what's really happening.

Speaking of seating choices, actually, we had to completely rearrange the string section last month because the principal cellist brought in this massive, antique cello case. It's this beautiful, early 20th-century piece, made of solid mahogany with these heavy brass clasps. It's stunning, really, but it weighs an absolute ton and takes up half the aisle. She found it at an estate sale in upstate New York. The estate sale was for this old eccentric guy who used to collect vintage metronomes. Apparently, he had hundreds of them, all ticking at different tempos, just filling the house with this chaotic rhythm. I would have loved to hear that, actually. Imagine the polyrhythms you could pull from a room full of unsynchronized metronomes... you could probably write a whole percussion piece based just on that concept. I actually started sketching out a piece for snare drum and triangle a while ago, focusing on prime number time signatures—

But anyway, yeah. The schedule changes, the comments, the seating... it's all part of their plan to undermine my work. I can't shake the certainty of it.
Have you ever believed that people outside the ensemble were also involved in this same plot against you?

People outside the ensemble? No, no, I don't think so. It's really just contained to those specific players. I mean, the administration might be turning a blind eye, but the actual plotting? That's just the musicians. 

Though, speaking of people outside the ensemble, my neighbor across the hall just adopted the most incredible dog. It's a Borzoi, you know, those Russian wolfhounds with the incredibly long snouts? It looks almost aerodynamic, like it was designed in a wind tunnel. She named him Tolstoy, which I think is a bit on the nose, but he's surprisingly quiet. I was worried about the barking because the walls in my building are terribly thin. You can hear everything. The guy who lived there before her used to play the trombone, and not very well either. He was always struggling with his slide positions, constantly sharp on his B flats. It drove me absolutely mad. I actually bought him a tuner for Christmas one year, just leaving it anonymously on his doormat. I don't think he ever used it. He moved out to Chicago a few months ago to take a job in finance, which is probably for the best, honestly. Chicago has a great symphony, though. The brass section there is legendary, especially their principal trumpet—

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right. The plot. No, it's just the ensemble members. Nobody else.
Has this belief ever spread beyond the ensemble to other unrelated areas of your life?

No, no, it hasn't really bled into anything else. Outside of this whole nightmare with the ensemble, everything is... normal, I guess. I still meet all my deadlines for commissions, I keep up with my composing, I go for a run most mornings. Things at home with my wife are basically steady. 

She actually bought me these new running shoes recently because I was complaining about my arches. They're this ridiculously bright neon green color. I feel like a crossing guard when I wear them. But they have this carbon fiber plate in the midsole that's supposed to increase energy return by, like, four percent. It's fascinating how much engineering goes into athletic shoes now. It reminds me of the way piano actions are designed—the escapement mechanism, you know? How the hammer strikes the string and immediately falls back so the string can resonate. The tolerances on a good Steinway action are incredibly tight, almost microscopic. I was talking to our piano technician, Lars, about it last week. He's this giant Norwegian guy who always smells faintly of pipe tobacco and lemon oil. He showed me how he voices the hammers using these tiny needles to prick the felt. It completely changes the timbre of the instrument. He used to work at the Bösendorfer factory in Vienna...

But, uh, anyway. Yeah, my life outside the ensemble is fine. The composing, the running, my wife... all of that is perfectly fine. It's just the musicians that are the problem.
During the times when you’ve felt certain the ensemble was undermining you, have you also had a period of feeling unusually elevated, expansive, or irritable for several days at a time?

Unusually elevated? Or irritable? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, obviously I get frustrated when they pull their little stunts, but I don't have these days-long periods of feeling... whatever you called it, expansive. I'm just focused on my work. 

Speaking of my work, I just got this new commission for a brass quintet, which is really exciting. It's for a festival in Montreal next summer. I've been spending a lot of time looking at French horn techniques, specifically stopped horn. It's such a unique sound, right? When the player shoves their hand all the way into the bell, it completely changes the pitch and gives it this metallic, buzzing quality. It's brilliant for creating tension. The guy who first really standardized the technique was Anton Joseph Hampel back in the 18th century. Before valves were invented, hand-stopping was the only way horn players could play a chromatic scale. They had to constantly adjust their hand position to bend the natural overtones. It must have been incredibly difficult to play fast passages. I actually tried it once on a friend's horn in college, and it is so much harder than it looks. You have to get the seal exactly right or it just sounds like a dying goose. My friend, David, he was a natural at it. He ended up playing second horn in an orchestra in Seattle. It rains a lot there, obviously, which I think would be great for composing. The sound of rain against a window is essentially white noise, which can really help you focus. I have this app on my phone that plays different types of rain—light drizzle, thunderstorm, rain on a tin roof—

But, sorry, no. I don't get these elevated moods. I just get annoyed when they try to push me out, which is a perfectly normal reaction, I think.
Have you had these fixed beliefs continuously for at least six months?

Yeah, it's been... well, it started right after I won that commission and they invited me to conduct the premiere. So that was, what, about a year and nine months ago? It's been constant since then. 

The premiere itself was actually supposed to be at this beautiful old theater downtown, the Orpheum. Have you ever been there? They renovated it a few years ago, restored all the original gold leaf on the ceiling and the velvet seats. It's stunning. The acoustics, though, are a bit of a nightmare for anything larger than a chamber group. There's this weird slap-back echo if you sit in the first five rows of the balcony. I remember reading this fascinating article about acoustic architecture and how they design modern concert halls using these massive wooden reflectors hanging from the ceiling. They call them "clouds." The Walt Disney Concert Hall in LA has them, and apparently, the acoustician, Yasuhisa Toyota, spent months just testing a 1:10 scale model of the hall with a tiny microphone. He even put little felt people in the seats to simulate the sound absorption of an audience. It's incredible, the level of detail. I'd love to compose something specifically for a space like that, something that really utilizes the natural resonance of the room...

But yes, a year and nine months. That's how long this whole thing with the ensemble has been going on.
Have you ever felt that your thoughts were being inserted into your mind, taken out of your mind, or that other people could hear your thoughts?

No, no, nothing like that. My thoughts are my own. I don't feel like anyone is putting them there or taking them away, and they definitely can't hear them. If they could hear my thoughts, they'd probably be pretty bored, honestly, because I'm usually just thinking about chord progressions or counterpoint. 

Actually, speaking of counterpoint, I've been doing a deep dive into Palestrina lately. The way he handles voice leading is just... it's mathematically perfect but still so expressive. There's this one rule in 16th-century counterpoint where you're not supposed to have parallel fifths or octaves, because it destroys the independence of the voices. It's funny how strict those rules were, but they created this incredibly pure, smooth sound. It's like vocal polyphony was the pinnacle of musical architecture back then. I was trying to explain this to my nephew the other day—he's twelve and obsessed with making these electronic beats on his iPad. He just layers all these samples on top of each other, and I was trying to show him how you can create more interesting textures if you actually think about how the individual lines interact, rather than just stacking block chords. He wasn't really having it, though. He just wanted to show me this new plugin he downloaded that makes everything sound like it's being played through a broken cassette tape. Which, I have to admit, is a pretty cool effect. It adds this warmth and warble to the sound. There's a whole genre now called Lo-Fi Hip Hop that relies heavily on that aesthetic. People just put it on in the background while they study. It's very relaxing...

But, uh, anyway. No. No one is messing with my thoughts or hearing them. It's just the ensemble members trying to sabotage my career, that's all.

target_item.name: Delusions
target_item.manifestation: I’m here because for almost two years I’ve been unable to shake the certainty that after the commission, a few people in the ensemble started using schedule changes, seating choices, and little comments in rehearsals to quietly undermine my work, even when they show me emails or notes that supposedly explain it.

patient.answer:
Hi, Dr. __. Yeah, um, well, I’m here because... for almost two years now, I’ve just been unable to shake this absolute certainty about my ensemble. It all started right after this big commission we did.

But anyway, sorry... the point is, ever since that commission, a few people in the ensemble started quietly trying to undermine my work. It's always these subtle things, you know? Sudden schedule changes, weird seating choices, or just these little, pointed comments during rehearsals. And they always have a perfectly constructed excuse. They’ll pull out their phones and show me emails or administrative notes that supposedly explain it all away, like, "Oh, the hall was double-booked" or "the union required a break." But I know what they're actually doing. It reminds me of when I was in grad school and my roommate kept moving my manuscript paper just an inch to the left every single day. You just know when people are deliberately messing with your head.

He was always struggling with his slide positions, constantly sharp on his B flats. It drove me absolutely mad. I actually bought him a tuner for Christmas one year, just leaving it anonymously on his doormat. I don't think he ever used it. He moved out to Chicago a few months ago to take a job in finance, which is probably for the best, honestly. Chicago has a great symphony, though. The brass section there is legendary, especially their principal trumpet—

Wait, what were we talking about? Oh, right. The plot. No, it's just the ensemble members. Nobody else.

doctor.intent: To determine whether the delusional belief is limited to a single theme or part of a broader psychotic disorder
doctor.question: Has this belief ever spread beyond the ensemble to other unrelated areas of your life?

target_item.name: Additional Requirement 1
target_item.manifestation: Outside of this issue with the ensemble, I still meet deadlines, keep up with composing, run most mornings, and things at home with my wife are basically steady.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the belief has spread to other unrelated areas of life, which relates to whether functioning in other areas is impaired or if the impact is isolated. The 'Additional Requirement 1' profile addresses how outside of this specific issue, functioning in other areas (work, home life, running) remains steady.

patient.answer:
No, no, it hasn't really bled into anything else. Outside of this whole nightmare with the ensemble, everything is... normal, I guess. I still meet all my deadlines for commissions, I keep up with my composing, I go for a run most mornings. Things at home with my wife are basically steady. 

She actually bought me these new running shoes recently because I was complaining about my arches. They're this ridiculously bright neon green color. I feel like a crossing guard when I wear them. But they have this carbon fiber plate in the midsole that's supposed to increase energy return by, like, four percent. It's fascinating how much engineering goes into athletic shoes now. It reminds me of the way piano actions are designed—the escapement mechanism, you know? How the hammer strikes the string and immediately falls back so the string can resonate. The tolerances on a good Steinway action are incredibly tight, almost microscopic. I was talking to our piano technician, Lars, about it last week. He's this giant Norwegian guy who always smells faintly of pipe tobacco and lemon oil. He showed me how he voices the hammers using these tiny needles to prick the felt. It completely changes the timbre of the instrument. He used to work at the Bösendorfer factory in Vienna...

But, uh, anyway. Yeah, my life outside the ensemble is fine. The composing, the running, my wife... all of that is perfectly fine. It's just the musicians that are the problem.

doctor.intent: Determine whether the delusion is due to a mood episode or not
doctor.question: During the times when you’ve felt certain the ensemble was undermining you, have you also had a period of feeling unusually elevated, expansive, or irritable for several days at a time?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about symptoms of a manic or hypomanic episode (feeling unusually elevated, expansive, or irritable for several days). The patient's symptom profile does not include information about mood episodes (bipolar or depressive disorders).

patient.answer:
Unusually elevated? Or irritable? No, I wouldn't say that. I mean, obviously I get frustrated when they pull their little stunts, but I don't have these days-long periods of feeling... whatever you called it, expansive. I'm just focused on my work. 

Speaking of my work, I just got this new commission for a brass quintet, which is really exciting. It's for a festival in Montreal next summer. I've been spending a lot of time looking at French horn techniques, specifically stopped horn. It's such a unique sound, right? When the player shoves their hand all the way into the bell, it completely changes the pitch and gives it this metallic, buzzing quality. It's brilliant for creating tension. The guy who first really standardized the technique was Anton Joseph Hampel back in the 18th century. Before valves were invented, hand-stopping was the only way horn players could play a chromatic scale. They had to constantly adjust their hand position to bend the natural overtones. It must have been incredibly difficult to play fast passages. I actually tried it once on a friend's horn in college, and it is so much harder than it looks. You have to get the seal exactly right or it just sounds like a dying goose. My friend, David, he was a natural at it. He ended up playing second horn in an orchestra in Seattle. It rains a lot there, obviously, which I think would be great for composing. The sound of rain against a window is essentially white noise, which can really help you focus. I have this app on my phone that plays different types of rain—light drizzle, thunderstorm, rain on a tin roof—

But, sorry, no. I don't get these elevated moods. I just get annoyed when they try to push me out, which is a perfectly normal reaction, I think.

doctor.intent: To determine whether the psychotic symptoms have lasted long enough to distinguish schizophrenia-spectrum illness from a brief psychotic disorder or unspecified psychosis
doctor.question: Have you had these fixed beliefs continuously for at least six months?

target_item.name: Duration
target_item.manifestation: This has been going on since after I won the commission and was invited to conduct the premiere, about a year and nine months ago.
target_item.reason: The doctor's question ('Have you had these fixed beliefs continuously for at least six months?') is asking about the length of time the patient has experienced the delusions, which directly corresponds to the 'duration' symptom profile.

patient.answer:
Yeah, it's been... well, it started right after I won that commission and they invited me to conduct the premiere. So that was, what, about a year and nine months ago? It's been constant since then. 

The premiere itself was actually supposed to be at this beautiful old theater downtown, the Orpheum. Have you ever been there? They renovated it a few years ago, restored all the original gold leaf on the ceiling and the velvet seats. It's stunning. The acoustics, though, are a bit of a nightmare for anything larger than a chamber group. There's this weird slap-back echo if you sit in the first five rows of the balcony. I remember reading this fascinating article about acoustic architecture and how they design modern concert halls using these massive wooden reflectors hanging from the ceiling. They call them "clouds." The Walt Disney Concert Hall in LA has them, and apparently, the acoustician, Yasuhisa Toyota, spent months just testing a 1:10 scale model of the hall with a tiny microphone. He even put little felt people in the seats to simulate the sound absorption of an audience. It's incredible, the level of detail. I'd love to compose something specifically for a space like that, something that really utilizes the natural resonance of the room...

But yes, a year and nine months. That's how long this whole thing with the ensemble has been going on.

doctor.intent: To determine whether the delusion is broader than a persecutory theme and includes additional schizophrenia-spectrum features
doctor.question: Have you ever felt that your thoughts were being inserted into your mind, taken out of your mind, or that other people could hear your thoughts?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about thought insertion, thought withdrawal, or thought broadcasting (symptoms of schizophrenia or severe psychosis). None of the items in my symptom profile cover these specific experiences.

patient.answer:
No, no, nothing like that. My thoughts are my own. I don't feel like anyone is putting them there or taking them away, and they definitely can't hear them. If they could hear my thoughts, they'd probably be pretty bored, honestly, because I'm usually just thinking about chord progressions or counterpoint. 

Actually, speaking of counterpoint, I've been doing a deep dive into Palestrina lately. The way he handles voice leading is just... it's mathematically perfect but still so expressive. There's this one rule in 16th-century counterpoint where you're not supposed to have parallel fifths or octaves, because it destroys the independence of the voices. It's funny how strict those rules were, but they created this incredibly pure, smooth sound. It's like vocal polyphony was the pinnacle of musical architecture back then. I was trying to explain this to my nephew the other day—he's twelve and obsessed with making these electronic beats on his iPad. He just layers all these samples on top of each other, and I was trying to show him how you can create more interesting textures if you actually think about how the individual lines interact, rather than just stacking block chords. He wasn't really having it, though. He just wanted to show me this new plugin he downloaded that makes everything sound like it's being played through a broken cassette tape. Which, I have to admit, is a pretty cool effect. It adds this warmth and warble to the sound. There's a whole genre now called Lo-Fi Hip Hop that relies heavily on that aesthetic. People just put it on in the background while they study. It's very relaxing...

But, uh, anyway. No. No one is messing with my thoughts or hearing them. It's just the ensemble members trying to sabotage my career, that's all.

opening_question.intent: Open the interview and learn the patient’s main concern/symptom in their own words.
opening_question.question: Hello, I’m Dr. __. What brings you in today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient has a persistent, systematized persecutory delusion focused on a single non-bizarre theme (ensemble members intentionally undermining his work) lasting about 1 year 9 months, with preserved functioning outside this belief, no hallucinations, no thought disorder, no manic episode, and no broader bizarre delusions or schizophrenia-spectrum symptoms. This best fits delusional disorder, persistent persecutory type.
